title: JOIN: combining related tables

spans.text: “JOIN: combining related tables” is a tool for solving a concrete programming problem. Identify the input and desired result, then trace what role the construct plays in the example. Study it not only as syntax, but also for its effects on readability, correctness, resource use, and future changes.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.

spans.code:
SELECT s.name, e.course_id
FROM students AS s
LEFT JOIN enrollments AS e
  ON e.student_id = s.student_id
ORDER BY s.name, e.course_id;

spans.text: All students appear; course_id is NULL for a student with no enrollment.

JOIN combines related tables. INNER JOIN keeps matching pairs; LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills missing right-side values with NULL. ON states the relationship explicitly. In a one-to-many relationship, one left row can produce several result rows.

Key line: `SELECT s.name, e.course_id`
What it does: All students appear; course_id is NULL for a student with no enrollment.
Why it is used: State join keys explicitly and predict how many matches each row can have.
If omitted or changed: RIGHT and FULL JOIN support varies by engine; LEFT JOIN is broadly supported.

spans.title: Common mistake
spans.text: A missing or incorrect ON condition can create many unintended pairs and inflate the result.
